newsitem.title: TURKEY: Turkey's Ciller suggests early elections.
newsitem.headline: Turkey's Ciller suggests early elections.

text.p: Turkish coalition ally Tansu Ciller on Wednesday suggested holding early polls to clear a political deadlock which is hampering the Islamist-led government and has badly damaged her pro-Western party.
"An agenda with elections at the top of it has emerged. The solution is with the people," Ciller told a meeting of deputies from her True Path Party (DYP).
Ciller's wing of the coalition has been steadily crumbling since the army began pushing Prime Minister Necmettin Erbakan to crack down on Islamist activism in February.
"Whatever we do, let's do it together," she said.
The True Path is to hold an executive meeting on Thursday to debate quitting the alliance. "Our party's bodies will meet in the days ahead and everything will become clear," Ciller said.

Ciller is expected to ask the party for the authority to threaten Erbakan with pulling out of the coalition if he does not hand over power to her soon to take the country to early elections. Polls are due by 2000 under normal circumstances.
State-run Anatolian news agency reported a right-wing party leader as saying Ciller and Welfare Party (RP) leader Erbakan had met him together and asked him to join their coalition.

The agency quoted Grand Union Party (BBP) leader Muhsin Yazicioglu as telling it via an aide: "At the three-way meeting, the BBP leader received an official offer to join the government from the leaders of the DYP and RP."

Yazicioglu said his party would consider the offer after "certain problems" within the coalition had been resolved. The support of six BBP deputies helped the coalition to narrowly survive a censure motion in parliament last week.
Analysts say Ciller, who has held leading government posts since becoming Turkey's first woman prime minister in 1993, wants to stay in office to ward off possible corruption charges.
However, she may not be able to hold off pressure from many of her MPs who favour snap elections or a secularist alliance to squeeze the Islamists from power.

"Tansu Ciller is trapped. She can't go right or left, back or forward," columnist Ismet Berkan wrote in the Radikal daily. "She is condemned to staying in office. Whatever she does she has to stay in power," he said.
Erbakan and Ciller are to swop jobs next year under a power-sharing deal that established their alliance last June.
U.S.-educated technocrat Ciller argues she can deflect the army's wrath from the government if she takes over as prime minister earlier and promises elections next spring.
Ciller, previously a strong critic of Welfare, helped the Islamists to power last year after they began presenting damaging graft dossiers against her to parliament.
Erbakan's Islam-based Welfare Party only narrowly won the last general elections in late 1995 with 21 percent of the vote and was struggling to find coalition partners.
Its voter support is reckoned to have grown since then.
Army criticism has forced three True Path ministers and a handful of MPs to quit the party in the last month.
The secularist generals, who have staged three coups since 1960, are angry that Erbakan has taken few concrete steps to reverse an upsurge in Islamist sentiment.
They say their fight against Islamists is a matter of "life or death" for NATO member Turkey and have inspired a strong legal bid to ban Welfare for allegedly threatening secularism.
Three MPs who resigned from Ciller's faction joined the main opposition Motherland Party in a ceremony on Wednesday.

The government has an absolute parliamentary majority on paper of just one but vacant seats give it a margin of four. A small right-wing grouping with seven members in the 550-seat assembly often backs Erbakan in key votes.
